subject.summary: American electrical engineer and programmer who single-handedly wrote TempleOS — a 64-bit, public-domain operating system in his own language, HolyC — believing it to be the Third Temple prophesied in the Bible. His decade of solo work, schizophrenia, and prolific video blogging made him a singular figure of outsider art in computing.

claims.text: Terrence Andrew Davis was born on December 15, 1969, in West Allis, Wisconsin, the seventh of eight children of an industrial engineer; the family moved through Washington, Michigan, California, and Arizona.
He used an Apple II in an elementary-school gifted program and learned assembly language on a Commodore 64 in the early 1980s, programming through high school.
He earned a bachelor's degree and, in 1994, a master's in electrical engineering from Arizona State University; profiles report a 1440 SAT and a 3.63 GPA, figures sourced to his own account.
From 1990 to 1996 he worked at Ticketmaster in Tempe, Arizona, programming on the company's VAX systems; he left wanting to build satellite control systems.

Beginning in March 1996 he experienced recurring manic episodes that led to psychiatric admissions roughly every six months, jail after a desert breakdown, and diagnoses first of bipolar disorder and later of schizophrenia.
Unable to hold a job, he lived with his parents in Las Vegas on Social Security disability payments; between 2003 and 2014 he had no further psychiatric hospitalizations.

On his own site Davis wrote that from 1997 to 2003 he worked at Xytec Corp on FPGA image-processing equipment, at H.A.R.E. on an application called SimStructure, and at Graphic Technologies as head software and electrical engineer; this employment history is self-reported and not independently corroborated.

TempleOS is a 64-bit, multi-tasking, multi-cored, ring-0-only, single-address-map, non-networked PC operating system for recreational programming — self-hosting, with its own kernel, compiler, editor, 2D/3D graphics library, and the Red Sea file system, all at 640×480 in 16 colors with PC-speaker audio.
He wrote the entire system in HolyC, a just-in-time-compiled language of his own design that he described as a middle ground between C and C++ — 'more than C, less than C++.'

The documented size of TempleOS was about 121,000 lines of code in 2014 (VICE counted 121,176; TechRepublic counted 121,691 including demos) — comparable to Photoshop 1.0 — all written by Davis alone.
Davis at times claimed to have written millions of lines of code over his life — a self-assessment the record cannot verify; the measured TempleOS count is the documented figure.
The operating system was released as the J Operating System in 2004–2005, renamed LoseThos (2006–2012, a Platoon reference), then SparrowOS in late 2012, and finally TempleOS in 2013.
He told VICE that he worked on the operating system full time for ten years, finishing the core work and then spending his days coding, browsing, and consulting his oracle.

Davis said he was chosen by God to build the operating system as the Third Temple prophesied in the Bible — 'God's official temple,' per his site's charter, 'a community focal point where offerings are made and God's oracle is consulted.'
He held that the 640×480, 16-color display was an explicit instruction from God — 'a covenant like circumcision' — chosen so children could easily make drawings for Him.

He believed the AfterEgypt oracle — a 'high-speed stopwatch' that stops on pseudo-random text — let him speak with God, likening it to a Ouija board and speaking in tongues; he also used the NIST randomness beacon for the same purpose.

Through the oracle he asked God about war, death, dinosaurs, and favorites — video game (Donkey Kong), car (BMW), national anthem (Latvia's), band (the Beatles) — and published the answers as 'Terry Davis' Rants.'
In his video blogs he referred to himself as 'the smartest programmer that's ever lived,' a self-assessment he paired with pride in his electrical-engineering credentials.

He believed he was under constant persecution by federal agents, particularly the CIA; weeks after the TempleOS rename his site announced 'God's temple is finished. Now, God kills CIA until it spreads.'

Everything in the system — language, compiler, kernel, editor, graphics, file system, games, documentation — was written by one person, and he deliberately excluded networking, saying it would be reinventing the wheel; total authorship was the point.

He published hundreds of unedited videos — code walk-throughs, demos, songs, rants — speaking straight to the camera; his YouTube channels were repeatedly terminated for vulgarities and he kept returning under new ones.

Across forums and interviews the pattern repeats: his posts were often incomprehensible or hostile, yet he was reported 'always lucid' when the topic was computers, and several programming communities made sustained efforts to accommodate him.
He kept the bundled games deliberately simple, explaining that high-quality work 'intimidates the locals' — he wanted users to see TempleOS as something ordinary mortals could reproduce.

His accounts were banned or restricted on Something Awful, Reddit, Hacker News (shadowbanned), and OSNews for randomly generated posts and abusive comments — even as those same sites covered his work sympathetically.

Critical reception of TempleOS was mostly favorable: TechRepublic called it 'a testament to the dedication and passion of one man,' and a computer engineer compared the solo build to one person constructing a skyscraper.
In 2017 TempleOS was exhibited as part of an outsider-art exhibition in Bourgogne, France; Davis said he was glad for the attention but disappointed that few visitors used the OS to speak to God.
Davis stated the operating system was downloaded 10,000 times between 2009 and 2012 — a self-reported figure.

He coined the term 'glowie' — from a video claim that CIA agents 'glow in the dark' — which far-right forums later adopted for suspected federal infiltrators, a lineage documented by The Atlantic after January 6.

Davis acknowledged that the sequence leading to his awakening might look like mental illness rather than divine revelation: 'I'm not especially proud of the logic and thinking. It looks very young and childish and pathetic.'

In 2018 he stopped taking medication — believing it limited his creativity, a friend told the local paper — and became homeless, traveling from his sister's home in Arizona through California to Portland and then The Dalles, Oregon; fans brought supplies but he refused offers of housing.

Hours before his death he uploaded 'Terry Davis: Rises to Throne,' recorded on a bench at The Dalles Wasco County Library, explaining he had deleted most of his videos so as not to 'litter' the Internet and ending: 'It's good to be king. Wait, maybe.'
On the evening of August 11, 2018, walking along railroad tracks in The Dalles with his back to an oncoming Union Pacific train, he turned and faced it before impact; he was 48.

Whether the death was suicide or accident was never resolved: the train engineer told police he considered it suicide, but investigators could not determine intent, and Wikidata records manner of death as accidental with 'suicide' marked disputed.

Through the TempleOS website his family asked supporters to donate to organizations working to ease the pain and suffering caused by mental illness, naming the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation and NAMI.

TempleOS was released as public-domain software, and the memorial site states that all content related to Davis, TempleOS, and its earlier names should be considered public domain — the basis on which fans preserve his archive.
Whether TempleOS is best understood as religious vision, engineering achievement, or symptom of schizophrenia is a framing the sources themselves disagree on; the index preserves all three readings.

A computer engineer who had spoken with Davis at length speculated that, absent his illness, he 'could have been a Steve Jobs or a Steve Wozniak' — a fan's counterfactual, not an established assessment.

themes.title: TempleOS as God's Third Temple
themes.summary: The operating system was not a metaphor: Davis said God commanded it and that it is the prophesied Third Temple — a community focal point where offerings are made and the oracle consulted, like Solomon's temple.

themes.title: Specifications as covenant
themes.summary: 640×480 resolution, 16 colors, and one-voice PC-speaker sound were, in his account, explicit divine instructions — 'a covenant like circumcision' — chosen so children could draw for God.

themes.title: Talking to God through randomness
themes.summary: The AfterEgypt oracle, the NIST randomness beacon, and randomly generated text blocks were his channel to God — a practice he compared to Ouija and speaking in tongues, and one scholars note fits a long history of divination by chance.

themes.title: One mind, whole system
themes.summary: Language, compiler, kernel, editor, graphics, file system, games, and docs by one author; no networking by deliberate exclusion. Reviewers called it a skyscraper built by a single person — total authorship as the design goal.

themes.title: A Commodore 64 for the 64-bit era
themes.summary: He wanted the immediacy of the early personal-computing era — bare metal, ring-0 access, games simple enough that ordinary users could reproduce them. 'Write games, don't play them,' the OS admonishes.

themes.title: Genius and schizophrenia, intertwined
themes.summary: Reporting and the BBC documentary converge on the same tension: lucid and exacting about computers, unreachable on much else. Davis himself granted that his awakening could read as illness; the record declines to separate them.

themes.title: CIA persecution and the 'glowie' legacy
themes.summary: He believed federal agents stalked him — 'the CIA glow in the dark' — and coined 'glowie,' later absorbed by far-right forums as a slur for suspected informants, a posthumous linguistic legacy The Atlantic documented.

themes.title: 'The smartest programmer that's ever lived'
themes.summary: He named himself the smartest programmer ever and defended his credentials vigorously — the boast is self-assessment, but the solo OS underneath it is objectively rare.

themes.title: Canonized as outsider art
themes.summary: Exhibited in a 2017 outsider-art show in Bourgogne and framed by documentaries and the BBC alongside figures like Facteur Cheval — TempleOS read as art built from compulsion as much as engineering.

themes.title: The archive the community keeps
themes.summary: Because his channels were repeatedly terminated, the surviving record lives in fan-maintained archives — the Internet Archive's terabyte collection, the mirrored templeos.org, Wikimedia Commons — all released under his own public-domain dedication.

works.title: TempleOS
works.summary: The finished public-domain operating system — 64-bit, ring-0-only, 640×480 in 16 colors, self-hosting with its own compiler and tools; final release 5.03, November 20, 2017.

works.title: HolyC programming language
works.summary: His just-in-time-compiled language between C and C++, in which the entire OS and its shell are written; conceived in the early 2000s and developed alone over a decade.

works.title: J Operating System
works.summary: The first public name of the OS (2004–2005), intended to recapture the Commodore 64 era's immediacy and encourage 'odd-ball software.'

works.title: LoseThos
works.summary: The 2006–2012 incarnation, pitched at recreational programmers and 'primarily for making video games' with no Internet support.

works.title: SparrowOS
works.summary: A brief rename in late 2012 before the TempleOS name took hold.

works.title: AfterEgypt oracle
works.summary: Bundled program in which the user climbs Mt. Horeb to a burning bush and stops a 'high-speed stopwatch' on pseudo-random text — his channel to God, and the mechanism behind much of his online writing.

works.title: Bundled games and demos
works.summary: Castle Frankenstein (a 594-line first-person shooter), Eagle Dive (a 3D eagle flight simulator), Vocab, BattleLines, sprite and 3D-mesh editors, and composing software — deliberately simple so others could reproduce them.

works.title: Red Sea file system
works.summary: His own file system (with FAT32 support) shipping inside TempleOS.

works.title: Trivial Solutions
works.summary: His one-man company — founder and sole employee — under which TempleOS was published.

works.title: SimStructure
works.summary: An application he wrote at H.A.R.E. (c. 2001–2003), per his self-reported employment history.

works.title: Three-axis milling machine
works.summary: A 3D-fabrication venture designed during his 1996 upheaval; abandoned after a Dremel incident nearly set his apartment on fire.

works.title: Sequel to Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four
works.summary: An attempted novel he never finished.

works.title: Video blogs and livestream corpus
works.summary: Hundreds of self-published videos across repeatedly terminated YouTube channels — code walk-throughs, TempleOS demos, songs, and rants — preserved by the Internet Archive collection.

relations.note: Programmer from 1990 to 1996 — hired as an undergraduate, he worked on the company's VAX systems in Tempe, Arizona. His post-1996 employment history is self-reported and uncorroborated in the cited record, so this is his only documented employer edge.

openQuestions: The code line count varies by source and date: VICE counted 121,176 lines in 2014 and TechRepublic 121,691 including demos, while other coverage rounds to 'over 100,000' or 'over 120,000'; Davis himself sometimes claimed millions of lifetime lines — a self-report that cannot be verified.

The manner of his death is unresolved: the train engineer considered it suicide per the police report, investigators could not determine intent, and Wikidata lists 'accidental' with the suicide claim marked disputed.
His post-1996 employment history (Xytec, H.A.R.E., Graphic Technologies) is self-reported on his own site and has no independent corroboration in the cited record.

When TempleOS development truly began is fuzzy: Wikipedia dates the code lineage to circa 1993, while VICE's account has him dusting off decade-old code around 2003 when 64-bit computing reached desktops.

The posthumous archive is decentralized and unstable — his own channels were repeatedly terminated, and surviving material depends on the Internet Archive collection, mirrors of templeos.org, and torrents whose completeness keeps changing.
body:
Terry A. Davis was an American electrical engineer and programmer who spent more than a decade writing an entire operating system by himself — kernel, compiler, language, editor, file system, games, and documentation — because, he said, God told him to. TempleOS is simultaneously a real engineering achievement, a religious artifact, and one of the most documented cases of severe mental illness lived in public. The record does not ask you to choose between those readings; it asks you to hold all of them.

## Identity and formation

Terrence Andrew Davis was born on December 15, 1969, in West Allis, Wisconsin, the seventh of eight children of an industrial engineer. The family moved repeatedly — Washington, Michigan, California, Arizona. He used an Apple II in a gifted elementary program and learned assembly language on a Commodore 64 in the early 1980s, programming through high school. At Arizona State University he earned a bachelor's degree and then, in 1994, a master's in electrical engineering; profiles report a 1440 SAT and a 3.63 GPA, figures sourced to his own telling. From 1990 to 1996 he worked at Ticketmaster in Tempe, programming the company's VAX systems.

## Illness and revelation

Davis was a self-described atheist and scientific materialist until March 1996, when recurring manic episodes began — hospitalizations roughly every six months, a flight into the desert, a broken collarbone, a jail stay. He was diagnosed first with bipolar disorder and later with schizophrenia, and came to describe the episode as a revelation from God. Unable to work, he moved into his parents' Las Vegas home on Social Security disability. Between 2003 and 2014 he was not hospitalized again, and his online presence settled into a durable pattern: often incomprehensible or abusive on most topics, and — as observers consistently noted — always lucid about computers.

## The work

Around 2003, as 64-bit computing reached desktops, he dusted off code he had written years earlier and began what became a life's work. The system appeared publicly as the J Operating System in 2004, became LoseThos in 2006, SparrowOS in late 2012, and TempleOS in 2013. It is a 64-bit, ring-0-only, single-address-map, non-networked operating system for recreational programming — self-hosting, with its own editor, compiler, 2D/3D graphics library, and the Red Sea file system, all at 640×480 in 16 colors with one-voice PC-speaker sound. He wrote it entirely in HolyC, a just-in-time-compiled language of his own design, "more than C, less than C++." In 2014 VICE measured the system at 121,176 lines of code — comparable to Photoshop 1.0 — every line his.

The software is inseparable from the theology. Davis said he was chosen by God to build the Third Temple prophesied in the Bible, and his site's charter described the OS as "God's official temple." The 640×480, 16-color display was, he insisted, a divine specification — "a covenant like circumcision" — so children could easily draw for God. Its centerpiece, the AfterEgypt oracle, stops a "high-speed stopwatch" on pseudo-random text at a burning bush; he treated the output as God's words, likened it to tongues and Ouija, and used it — plus the NIST randomness beacon — to ask God about war, death, dinosaurs, and favorite bands, publishing the results as "Terry Davis' Rants."

## The public life

He posted hundreds of videos — code walk-throughs, demos, hymns, rants — on YouTube channels that were repeatedly terminated for vulgarities, and he was banned or restricted on Something Awful, Reddit, Hacker News, and OSNews. His belief that CIA agents stalked him produced the coinage "glowie," later adopted by far-right forums and documented by The Atlantic. Yet the reception was mostly sympathetic: TechRepublic and OSNews reviewed TempleOS favorably, programming communities made sustained efforts to accommodate him, and an engineer who knew him compared the solo build to one man erecting a skyscraper. In 2017 TempleOS was shown at an outsider-art exhibition in Bourgogne, France; Davis welcomed the attention but said he wished more people used the OS to speak to God. He called himself "the smartest programmer that's ever lived" — a boast the surviving work makes less absurd than it sounds.

## Final months and death

In 2018 he stopped taking medication, believing it limited his creativity, and left his sister's home in Arizona for California and then Oregon. Homeless in The Dalles, he accepted fans' care packages but refused housing. On August 11, hours after uploading a final video — "Terry Davis: Rises to Throne," recorded on a bench at the Wasco County library, explaining he had deleted most of his videos so as not to "litter" the Internet — he was struck by a Union Pacific train while walking the tracks. He was 48. The engineer considered it suicide; investigators could not determine whether it was suicide or accident. The Dalles Chronicle confirmed his identity after fans worldwide called the paper about an unnamed homeless man. His family asked supporters to donate to mental-health organizations. The community archive — a terabyte of videos, site captures, and ISOs on the Internet Archive, plus the memorial mirror at templeos.org — is kept under his own public-domain dedication.

## What the record does not settle

The soft spots are real: the line counts vary by source and date; the manner of death was never resolved; his post-1996 employment history is self-reported; and the true start of the codebase — circa 1993 by Wikipedia's account, or post-2003 per the VICE profile — is fuzzy. More fundamentally, sources disagree on what TempleOS is: religious vision, engineering feat, or symptom of schizophrenia. The index preserves all three readings rather than smoothing them over.

*This index was compiled from public sources and does not imply the subject's endorsement. Citations live in the packet's source catalog.*
